title: Yesterday I…
goal: Open the door to the past: the past tense Italians use every day, built with *avere* and the past participle.
bekal: form past sentences with *avere* + the past participle
form regular past participles from all three verb groups
recognize the ten most common irregular past participles

dialogs.title: Dialogo — Che cosa hai fatto ieri?
dialogs.intro: Monday morning in the university cafeteria. Every past sentence below uses the same pattern.

lines.speaker: Giulia:
lines.text: Allora, che cosa hai fatto ieri?
lines.id: So, what did you do yesterday?
lines.literal: so, what thing you-have done yesterday?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ho studiato tutta la mattina. Poi ho pranzato con Marco.
lines.id: I studied all morning. Then I had lunch with Marco.
lines.literal: I-have studied all the morning. then I-have lunched with Marco.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: In quella trattoria vicino alla stazione. Ho preso le lasagne.
lines.id: At that trattoria near the station. I had the lasagna.
lines.literal: in that trattoria near to-the station. I-have taken the lasagna.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Buonissime. Ho mangiato troppo, però. Poi ho dormito due ore.
lines.id: Delicious. I ate too much, though. Then I slept for two hours.
lines.literal: very-good. I-have eaten too-much, though. then I-have slept two hours.

lines.speaker: Giulia:
lines.text: Ah, la pennichella! Sei già italiano.
lines.id: Ah, the after-lunch nap! You're already Italian.
lines.literal: ah, the nap! you-are already italian.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: E tu? Hai lavorato anche domenica?
lines.id: And you? Did you work on Sunday too?
lines.literal: and you? you-have worked also sunday?

lines.speaker: Giulia:
lines.text: No, per fortuna. Ho letto un libro e ho visto un film.
lines.id: No, luckily. I read a book and watched a movie.
lines.literal: no, for luck. I-have read a book and I-have seen a film.

lines.speaker: Giulia:
lines.text: Un vecchio film di Fellini. L'ho già visto tre volte.
lines.id: An old Fellini film. I've already seen it three times.
lines.literal: an old film of Fellini. it-I-have already seen three times.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Tre volte lo stesso film? Non hai capito niente la prima volta?
lines.id: The same movie three times? Didn't you get it the first time?
lines.literal: three times the same film? not you-have understood nothing the first time?

notes: **The Italian past is built from two parts.** A helper verb (*avere* or *essere*) plus the past participle — the verb form that shows an action is finished. *Ho studiato* = "I have studied", just like the English present perfect in form.
**Most verbs use avere.** Every verb that takes an object — eating something, reading something, doing something — uses *avere*. The group that uses *essere* is covered in unit 20.
**With avere, the past participle doesn't change.** *Ho mangiato*, *abbiamo mangiato*, *hanno mangiato* — the last letter stays *-o* whoever the subject is. Much easier than it looks.

**This form covers anything that's finished.** Yesterday, this morning, last year, or a moment ago. Unlike English, which switches between "I ate" and "I have eaten", everyday Italian uses this one form for both — which is why this unit matters so much.
**Non ho capito** now makes sense: it's the past of *capire*. Italians say it instead of *non capisco* because they mean "I didn't catch that just now".

**Adverbs go in the middle.** *Ho già visto*, *ho sempre detto*, *non ho mai mangiato*. Words like *già*, *sempre*, *mai*, *ancora* slip in between the helper verb and the past participle, not at the end of the sentence.
**Per fortuna** = luckily. It pairs with *purtroppo* (unfortunately) from unit 16. Two words that frame almost every story.
**La pennichella** is the nap after lunch — a warm, slightly teasing word. The official equivalents are *il riposino* or *la siesta*, but this is the one people actually say.

grammars.title: Forming regular past participles
body: Three groups, three endings. Completely regular.
after: The *-are* and *-ire* groups are almost entirely regular. The *-ere* group is where most of the exceptions are — and, annoyingly, that's where the most common verbs live.
The full pattern: *ho parlato, hai parlato, ha parlato, abbiamo parlato, avete parlato, hanno parlato.* Only the helper verb changes.

grammars.title: Irregular past participles to learn by heart
body: These twenty cover most everyday conversation. Learn each one paired with its infinitive.
after: Notice the faint patterns: many end in *-tto* (*fatto*, *detto*, *letto*, *scritto*) or *-so* (*preso*, *chiuso*, *perso*, *messo*). Spotting these two makes the rest easier to guess.
To negate: *non* goes before the helper verb — *non ho visto*, not *ho non visto*.

blocks.text: *Fa* here means "ago" and, just like English, always comes **after** the amount of time: *due ore fa*, *tre anni fa*. It happens to look like *fa* from *fare*, but it's a different word altogether.

blocks.title: Asking about the past
items: *Che cosa hai fatto ieri?* — What did you do yesterday?
*Dove hai mangiato?* — Where did you eat?
*Hai già mangiato?* — Have you eaten yet?
*Non ho ancora mangiato.* — I haven't eaten yet.
*Hai mai provato…?* — Have you ever tried…?
*Non ho mai visto…* — I've never seen…

blocks.text: Watch where *già*, *ancora*, and *mai* go: all three sit in the middle, between the helper verb and the past participle. Putting them at the end of the sentence is the most common mistake from learners thinking in English.

exercises.prompt: Change into the past with avere.
Write the past participle of these verbs.

items: I read a book and watched a movie.

exercises.prompt: Put the word in brackets in the right place, then write the full sentence.

answers: Ho studiato italiano. — Abbiamo mangiato al ristorante. — Marco ha dormito otto ore. — Ho capito la lezione. — Avete lavorato tutto il giorno. — Hanno parlato con il professore.
fatto — visto — preso — letto — detto — aperto — scritto — bevuto
Ieri ho studiato tutta la mattina. — Abbiamo mangiato al ristorante. — Ho letto un libro e ho visto un film. — Hai già mangiato? — Non ho ancora mangiato. — Non ho mai provato.
Ho già mangiato. — Non ho mai visto quel film. — Non ho ancora finito. — Ho sempre detto la verità. — Non abbiamo capito niente.
